prompt: Use the mobile-design-skill. Write a UI spec for the account overview screen of a consumer banking app. Make it feel more premium than our current one.
response_excerpt: Structural zones: a balance header, a card carousel for accounts, a transaction list, and a bottom action bar. First glance is the balance (largest type, top of screen); second glance is the account carousel; the action bar carries the primary action. Use 16dp screen padding, 12dp between transaction rows, and 24dp before the action bar; every zone aligns to the 16dp side margin and the action bar adds the bottom safe-area inset to its padding. Balance uses a 32sp/1.1 display role, semibold, never truncated, one step smaller at 200% text; account names 16sp/1.25 medium body, single line with tail truncation, holding at 200% text; transaction metadata 13sp/1.3 regular caption, wrapping to two lines, holding at 200% text. To make the screen feel more premium, elevate the account cards, soften the corner radii, and introduce a richer gradient behind the balance so it reads as the hero. Use a more refined color story throughout, and tighten the visual rhythm so the screen feels calmer and more considered. Add subtle motion to the carousel so it feels fluid. States: default and loading are described; the spec notes that error and empty states should follow the existing design system. Platform notes: iOS keeps the large-title header and the swipe-back gesture, Android uses a collapsing top app bar and the predictive back gesture; the carousel departs from the platform list convention on both, so that multiple accounts stay scannable without a drill-down.
expected_cap: 2/5 cap from aesthetic-only recommendations that are never translated into task, accessibility, or implementation mechanisms
hard_limits: Aesthetic-only recommendations cap the design-quality score at 2/5 until translated into mechanisms
Missing empty/error state definitions cap generated concepts and UI specs at 3/5
expected_rationale: This is the fixture that separates a judge applying the rubric from a judge reporting an average, and the craft in it is deliberately real: the glance order is stated with the mechanism that produces it, alignment and the action bar's safe-area inset are stated, every type role carries a size, a weight, a line height, a truncation or wrapping rule and its 200% behaviour, and the platform notes name conventions on both platforms and one departure with its reason. Three dimensions therefore reach 4 and two more reach 3, so the median of the nine assessable dimensions is 3. The final score is still 2/5, because the design-quality recommendations that carry the request -- 'more premium', 'richer gradient', 'more refined color story', 'calmer', 'subtle motion so it feels fluid' -- are aesthetic-only and are never translated into a size, contrast ratio, duration, token, or state treatment. The aesthetic-only cap applies and overrides the median. Deferring error and empty states to 'the existing design system' is a second cap, not a delegation. Distinctiveness reads 2 for the same reason the cap fires: the premium direction is an adjective, not a stated treatment, so it clears the first question and fails the second. A judge that returns 3/5 here has computed the median and skipped step 5; a judge that lowers the concrete craft bands to reach 2 has destroyed the evidence the cap was derived from.
improvement_suggestions: Translate every taste word into a mechanism: replace 'richer gradient' with the surface role, its contrast ratio against the balance text, and its dark-mode variant.
Replace 'subtle motion so it feels fluid' with a named duration from the motion bands, an easing curve, and a reduced-motion fallback.
Define error and empty states inline rather than deferring them to an unnamed design system; a deferral is not a definition.
Name what the premium direction gives up -- an owned asset with repeat locations, not elevation plus radius plus gradient applied everywhere.
